Euler's totient function. Denoted as phi of n, it counts how many positive integers up to n are relatively prime to n, meaning they share no common factors other than one. Euler proved a remarkable generalization of Fermat's Little Theorem: if gcd of a and n equals one, then a to the power of phi of n is congruent to one modulo n. This function is indispensable to modern cryptography, underpinning RSA key generation and the security of digital commerce.

Phi of n counts integers k where k lies between one and n and gcd of k and n equals one. Equivalently, phi of n is the order of the multiplicative group of units modulo n. For a prime p, phi of p equals p minus one, since all nonzero residues modulo p are coprime to p, forming a cyclic group. For prime powers, phi of p to the k equals p to the k minus one times p minus one, accounting for multiples of p in the range from one to p to the k.

The Euler totient function has a multiplicative property. If gcd of m and n equals one, then phi of m times n equals phi of m times phi of n. This makes the function fundamental to multiplicative number theory. The Euler totient function satisfies a remarkable identity: the sum of phi of d over all divisors d of n equals n. This is a consequence of counting residue classes.

Phi of n generalizes Fermat's Little Theorem. For gcd of a and n equals one, a to the power of phi of n is congruent to one modulo n. This is Euler's theorem, proven using group theory. The totient function is critical for RSA cryptography. Public key generation requires computing phi of the product p times q, which equals p minus one times q minus one, where p and q are secret primes. The security of RSA hinges on factoring being computationally hard. In practice, the totient is never computed by factoring. Instead, n is chosen as a product of large primes so that factoring n remains computationally infeasible, securing RSA's secrecy. Applications of phi of n extend beyond cryptography to Möbius inversion, counting primitive roots, and Carmichael's theorem on universal exponents.
